vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to tell somebody about a possible problem before it happens
using exactly the same words that another person said
to pass a message or information from one person to another
to accept or say that something is true
comments about how good or bad a piece of work is, so that it can improve
to ask somebody very strongly to do something
to tell somebody to remember something that they need to do
to say that something is especially important

paras: Ana Ferreira leads the reporting team in a shared service center, and half of her job, she says, is passing on messages that are not hers. A director gives feedback in a call in English. Ana has to relay it to six analysts and to a BPO team in another country, often the same afternoon. And she has noticed something: by the third person, the message has changed.

The problem is not that people forget the facts. It is the verb. Somebody writes the director said the deadline is important, and the BPO does not know if that is a fact, a request or a warning. Nobody knows what to do with it, so nobody does anything, and on Friday the pack is late.

Ana now asks her team to choose the verb before they write. Did the director remind us to do something we already knew? Did she warn us about a risk? Did she urge us to act this week? Did she stress that one point was fixed, or only suggest a change? And when a director acknowledges that something went well, Ana relays that too, because good news travels badly in a long email.

Her last rule is the hardest for new analysts: do not repeat the call word for word. Nobody reads a transcript. Three lines, with the right verb in each one, tell the team what is fixed, what is a request, and when. The director stressed that the pack must go out on Friday. She asked us to send the bank statements by Wednesday. That is a relay. Everything else is noise.

gist.prompt: What is this text mainly about?
choices: Why analysts should write a full transcript of every call, so that the BPO in the other country does not miss any of the director's words.

Why directors give too much feedback.

listenings.text: I lead a team of twelve at the BPO in Buenos Aires, and most of our instructions arrive second hand. The director speaks to the client, the client speaks to my contact, and my contact writes to me. By then, the message has often changed. Last month I received: they said the deadline is important. That is true, but it does not help me. What I need is the verb. Did they remind us, or did they warn us? Did they ask us to change something, or only suggest it? A good relay sounds like this: the director stressed that the pack must go out on Friday, and she asked you to send the bank statements by Wednesday. Now I know what is fixed, what is a request, and when. I do not need the call word for word. I need the main message and the right verb.

I am a controller, and I give feedback to three countries every month. I speak quickly in those calls, and I know that not everybody catches everything. So I always ask one person in each country to relay the main points to the team. The ones who do it well never write a transcript. They write three lines. The controller acknowledged that the March numbers were better. He urged us to close the open items before the fifth. He suggested reviewing the accruals with the BPO every week. That is all. When I read a relay like that, I know my message arrived. And if I see the word said five times, I know the team will have to call me again to ask what I actually wanted.
